source_text:
Apophthegmata
Περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Ἐπιφανίου ἐπισκόπου Κύπρου.
αʹ. ∆ιηγήσατο ὁ ἅγιος Ἐπιφάνιος ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, ὅτι ἐπὶ τοῦ μακαρίου
Ἀθανασίου τοῦ μεγάλου, κορῶναι περιϊπτάμεναι τὸ τοῦ Σεράπιδος ἱερὸν, ἔκραζον
ἀπαύ 65.164 στως, Κρᾶς, Κρᾶς. Καὶ προστάντες ἐπὶ τὸν μακάριον Ἀθανάσιον οἱ
Ἕλληνες, ἔκραξαν· Κακόγηρε, εἰπὲ ἡμῖν τί κράζουσιν αἱ κορῶναι. Καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς
εἶπεν· Αἱ κορῶναι κράζουσι, Κρᾶς, Κρᾶς· τὸ δὲ Κρᾶς τῇ Αὐσωνίων φωνῇ αὔριόν ἐστι
καὶ προσετίθει, ὅτι Αὔριον ὄψεσθε τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Καὶ ἑξῆς ἠγγέλθη ὁ θάνατος
τοῦ Ἰουλιανοῦ βασιλέως. Καὶ τούτου γενομένου, συνδραμόντες κατέκραζον τοῦ
Σεράπιδος, λέγοντες· Ἐὰν οὐκ ἤθελες αὐτὸν, τί ἐλάμβανες τὰ αὐτοῦ;
βʹ. Ὁ αὐτὸς διηγήσατο, ὅτι ἦν τις ἡνίοχος κατὰ τὴν Ἀλεξανδρέων, ὃς ἦν
μητρὸς Μαρίας υἱός. Οὗτος ἱππικοῦ ἐπιτελουμένου κατέπεσεν· εἶτα ἀναστὰς
παρῆλθε τὸν καταβεβληκότα, καὶ ἐνίκησε. Καὶ τὸ πλῆθος ἀνεβόησεν· Ὁ Υἱὸς Μαρίας
πέπτωκε καὶ ἐγήγερται καὶ ἐνίκησε. Ταύτης ἔτι τῆς φωνῆς λεγομένης, ἐνέπεσεν ἡ
περὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ τοῦ Σεράπιδος φήμη τῷ πλήθει, ὅτι ὁ μέγας Θεόφιλος ἀνελθὼν, τὸ
τοῦ Σεράπιδος κατέστρεψεν εἴδωλον, καὶ τοῦ ναοῦ γέγονεν ἐγκρατής.
γʹ. Ἐδηλώθη τῷ μακαρίῳ Ἐπιφανίῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ Κύπρου παρὰ τοῦ ἀββᾶ τῆς
μονῆς ἧς εἶχεν ἐν Παλαιστίνῃ, ὅτι Εὐχαῖς σου οὐκ ἠμελήσαμεν τοῦ κανόνος ἡμῶν,
ἀλλὰ μετὰ σπουδῆς καὶ τὴν τρίτην καὶ τὴν ἕκτην καὶ τὴν ἐννάτην ἐπιτελοῦμεν.
thought_title: Crows, a charioteer, and the fall of the Serapeum
orientation: The collection opens with Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, telling stories about the fall of the Serapeum and the death of Julian, then a report from his monastery in Palestine.
pass_a_gloss: Sayings. Concerning the holy Epiphanius bishop of Cyprus. 1. The holy Epiphanius the bishop related that in the time of the blessed Athanasius the Great, crows flying around the temple of Serapis were crying out without ceasing, 'Cras, Cras.' And the pagans, standing before the blessed Athanasius, cried out: 'Evil old man, tell us what the crows are crying.' And answering he said: 'The crows are crying, Cras, Cras; and Cras in the language of the Ausonians is tomorrow.' And he added, that 'Tomorrow you will see the glory of God.' And next the death of Julian the king was announced. And when this had happened, running together they were shouting against Serapis, saying: 'If you did not want him, why were you taking his things?' 2. The same one related that there was a certain charioteer in the city of the Alexandrians, who was the son of a mother Mary. This man, when a horse race was being held, fell; then rising he passed the one who had thrown him down, and won. And the crowd shouted: 'The Son of Mary has fallen and has risen and has won.' While this cry was still being said, the report about the temple of Serapis fell upon the crowd, that the great Theophilus, having gone up, destroyed the idol of Serapis, and became master of the temple. 3. It was made known to the blessed Epiphanius the bishop of Cyprus by the abba of the monastery which he had in Palestine, that 'By your prayers we have not neglected our rule, but with diligence we perform both the third and the sixth and the ninth.'

choices.why: Glossary requires 'pagans' for non-Christian worshippers of Serapis, not 'Greeks'.
The word is a Latin loanword transliterated into Greek; keeping the Latin form preserves the pun on 'tomorrow'.
Ausonians is the Greek term for Italians/Romans; a literal rendering preserves the source's ethnic term.
Glossary requires 'rule' for the appointed prayer hours, not 'office' or 'prayer rule'.
Dative of means; the monks attribute their diligence to Epiphanius's prayers.
The verb means to carry out or complete the appointed hours; 'perform' keeps the sense of fulfilling the rule.

pass_b_english: The holy bishop Epiphanius told this story: In the time of blessed Athanasius the Great, crows were flying around the temple of Serapis, crying out without stopping, "Cras, cras." The pagans came to blessed Athanasius and shouted, "Evil old man, tell us what the crows are crying." He answered, "The crows are crying, 'Cras, cras.' In the language of the Ausonians, 'cras' means 'tomorrow.'" And he added, "Tomorrow you will see the glory of God." The next day the death of the emperor Julian was announced. When this happened, they ran together and shouted against Serapis, saying, "If you did not want him, why did you take what was his?"

The same one told this story: There was a charioteer in Alexandria who was the son of a woman named Mary. During a horse race he fell. Then he got up, passed the one who had thrown him down, and won. The crowd shouted, "The son of Mary has fallen and has risen and has won." While this cry was still being said, the report about the temple of Serapis reached the crowd: the great Theophilus had gone up, destroyed the idol of Serapis, and become master of the temple.

It was reported to blessed Epiphanius, the bishop of Cyprus, by the abba of the monastery he had in Palestine: "By your prayers we have not neglected our rule, but with diligence we perform the third, the sixth, and the ninth hours."
notes: The source text contains 'ἀπαύ 65.164 στως' which appears to be OCR damage or a page/line reference inserted into the word ἀπαύστως ('without ceasing'). The gloss renders it as 'without ceasing' based on the visible letters.
